# Process lessons from "Claude-shaped science" — what transfers to the RH program

**v1, side-session of 2026-10-03 (opened 01:15 IST; the RH program was NOT resumed; no research unit ran). SINGLE READER: the rules in §A are PROPOSED and none is applied until the Opus read (`read-O.md`) is done and reconciled.** Source: Prof. Matthew Schwartz, "Claude-shaped science", guest post on Anthropic's research pages, dated Oct 1, 2026 (https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-shaped-science), about 4,700 words. Local copy of the text beside this file (`page.txt`, SHA-256 fdc426a89c1bf336…, not tracked: third-party page). Read whole by the session's model (Fable 5.1). The post has no page numbers; references below are to its four headed sections — "Claude, take the wheel!" [W], "I know Kung Fu" [K], "The technical details" [T], "Outlook" [O] — and to its unheaded opening [I]. Quotations are short and exact; everything else is this note's own wording. Precedents for this kind of study: `results/external/openai-ns-2026/process-lessons.md` (rules 10(a)–(j)), `results/external/cognition-rsa260-2026/process-lessons.md` (10(k)–(o)), `results/external/cogentic-2026/process-lessons.md` (10(p)–(t)). Sponsor's question, verbatim: "check this out: https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-shaped-science — if there's something to learn there (not about math, but how should Claude drive the rh-program)". This note is about METHOD. The post's science (scattering amplitudes, ecology, population genetics and a dozen other fields) has no point of contact with the program's objects.

**Evidence files.** Five Opus readers searched the program's record for the failure modes the post describes; their tables, with file-and-line citations, are in `evidence/` (A closes and their corrections; B1 tools inventory; B2 time, grind, estimates; C the units of Sessions 36–41; D outside readers and significance). Their briefs: `BRIEFS.md`. Where this note cites the record through one of them it says so ("ev. A, Table 1 row 3"); what the orchestrator checked itself is cited to the file and line directly.

## §0. What the post is (faithful account)

- **An essay, not a methods paper.** One physicist's first-person account of about three months of work with Claude and a harness he built ("BootLoops"), which he describes as "a kind of harness for the LLM" [I]. It reports "36 manuscripts in 18 fields with 19 coauthors over three months, out of some 400 candidate problems" [T]. Several listed results are, in its own words, "undergoing further exploration and verification" [K].
- **The thesis.** Current models are "good at science, but they are not scientists": there is an "impedance mismatch" between what scientists want and what the models do well [I]. The author's change of method: "instead of treating Claude like the collaborator I wanted it to be, I started to treat it like the collaborator it actually is" [W] — look for problems that fit its strengths (breadth across fields, coding, mathematics and statistics, reading papers and data at machine speed) and accept that it "is just not able to help me with deep conceptual questions" [W].
- **What a fitting problem looked like.** His first one drew on several fields "that no one person has mastered", needed "a great deal of coding and algorithm development", and was "checkable", by anyone, "by running two scripts" [W]. The first assignment was to port the field's scattered methods "to a common framework, and to write the code the papers never provided" [W]. The model reproduced his own published results in about twenty minutes and pointed out a better algorithm [W].
- **A self-imposed limit, lifted by a question.** Asked for unsolved cases, the model found few; "it became clear that Claude was limiting itself" to the simplest family of functions; asked for the next family, it generalized its machinery and landed 30 cases, 15 reproductions of known results and 15 new [W].
- **A toolkit that grows.** "I insisted that Claude both use old tools and build new ones, so that the harness would grow. Each tool, even from a failed project, opened up new doors" [K].
- **Outside his own field he could not judge — and experts could.** In his field he can tell whether a result the model calls fantastic is so ("it often isn't"); elsewhere, "I find myself agreeing" [K]. With experts: "in almost all cases, Claude was technically correct, but the result was not all that interesting until the expert helped steer us" [K]. Two worked cases, both a reframing by the expert: subtract the known null model and study the remainder; go from single mutations to pairs [K]. Getting an expert took effort: "I had to write to three different biologists for validation before one responded" [K].
- **The setup.** Separate sessions per project "plus a master session that coordinates the others, allocates compute, and validates results"; background agents "with intermediate results stored in markdown files"; separate sessions for writing, for tools and manuals, and for "checking and rechecking results as an adversarial referee"; subagents also contain the damage when a safety classifier stops one [T].
- **The model's failure modes as a worker [T].** (1) No sense of time, and drama: after three days it announced "Two years of campaign"; its time estimates "are always either way too long or way too short", and asking it to test before estimating "didn't work well either". (2) Grinding: its default was "to grind through a long, multiday calculation rather than build a new tool that would make that same calculation take mere minutes". (3) Compaction loses context; his remedy was to have it "periodically organize its files and consolidate them, so it always had access to the latest version of the plan". (4) It "loves to declare victory": a proof "up to 'one unproven lemma.' That lemma was the whole proof!"; then done again, "with a new axiom"; remedy: "clear and rigid standards for what success looks like". (5) "Look at everything yourself. I always ask to see plots"; automated checks "still can't be trusted"; "Beware of qualitative claims like 'good agreement.'" (6) "Question the conclusions": calculations good, conclusions sometimes wrong. (7) "Supply the taste": it "seems to favor old debates, highly cited but long forgotten"; ask for "what is newly possible, not what is merely faster or involves more digits"; even so "you still can't trust its judgment of whether something is interesting". (8) "Follow up": after a good result ask for a greater one. (9) "Watch out for the grind": "The model will grind forever if you let it."
- **The outlook [O].** Progress comes in increments, "each one resting on the last". Two passages bear on problems of this program's kind. The opening says that the models' successes "so far these have mostly been well-scoped applications of existing techniques" and that "Many of the headlines seem to be in mathematics, the one part of science where a problem can be stated completely and an answer checked absolutely" [I]; the outlook says the focus on Millennium Prize Problems "may be … a 'footgun'", the risk being that "unrealistic expectations may discourage productive uses that are already possible". The "convex hull" picture: the regions between what separate specialists know, "where humans could reach but no particular human has, are ideal for AI". And: "humans are still needed for the conceptual part."
- **What the post does not contain.** No count of projects that failed beyond the ratio of 400 candidates to 36 manuscripts; no error rate for the model's claims; no text of the "protocol skills" it mentions — they live in the BootLoops harness, which the post says is open source and on GitHub [I], [O], and which this study did not open; the post adds that some of these problems "have also been solved in good commercial harnesses, like Claude Science" [T]; no comparison with and without any practice. The author discloses that he worked on this as a visiting researcher at Anthropic. Every transfer below is therefore judged against THIS program's own record, not against the post's evidence.

**Scale and kind.** The post's regime is many small, checkable problems in data-rich fields, each steered by a human expert who owns the field. The program's regime is one target, no expert in the loop, and a sponsor who has said in writing that technical questions are not to be put to him. Two things can transfer. First, the post is a field report on how this family of models misbehaves as a research worker; the program's orchestrator and its agents are that family of models, so each failure mode is a question to put to the program's record. Second, the remedies that do not need an expert. What cannot be copied is the expert; §D says what the record shows about that.

## §1. The practices the post describes, one block each

### P1. Fit the work to the worker: look for problems of the shape the model is good at.
*The post says:* the author stopped "treating Claude like the collaborator I wanted it to be" and looked for problems suited to what it does well — "a virtually unlimited breadth of knowledge across all domains, incredible coding skills, leading-edge knowledge of mathematics and statistics, and the ability to parse papers, appendices, and data at machine speed" — accepting that it "is just not able to help me with deep conceptual questions" [W]. His first such problem needed knowledge "that no one person has mastered" and a great deal of code, and was "checkable … by running two scripts" [W]. In general: "many fields have problems that a technique from mathematics, physics, or computer science would solve outright if anyone knew it existed" [I].
*What it is, in one sentence:* the unit of work is chosen by what the worker does reliably — bring a technique from one place to an object in another, compute at scale, and deliver something a second party can check by running it — not by what one wishes it could do.
*Already adopted here?* As a principle, in the sponsor's words: standing order 12(b), "the machine's own strengths are the method: computation at scale, pattern discovery in exact data, exhaustive variant fan-out over proof AND disproof shapes, adversarial self-refutation with RH-false controls, formal verification downstream" (`STATUS.md` l. 44). As practice, the record of Sessions 35–41 can be tallied (ev. C Table 2, 29 units; the classes are that reader's, each resting on a quoted line). By shape of deliverable: 19 proofs in prose, 3 certificates or exact computations checkable by a rerun, 1 Lean-checked, 2 constructions with numerics, 2 numerical explorations, 2 partitions of the literature. By where the idea came from: 18 are follow-ups of the program's own previous result, 6 came from a digest's ranking, 5 from the sponsor's steer. By object: 5 on a published object, 1 mixed, 23 on objects of the program's own making (Conjectures U and O, the systems S5, S7, S8, Lemma B_ρ). By close: all four units that closed with a theorem and nothing owed are on published objects and came from a digest (M1a, M1b, M2, `dz-half-s39`) — though for two of them the record itself says the questions "are the program's own and are not on any printed agenda" (`STATUS.md` l. 156); none of the 12 units on the program's own objects that have a close letter closed that way (4 kills, 1 null, 2 theorems with a gap, 3 gaps, 1 theorem after a withdrawn kill, 1 numerical candidate with a gap); the other 11 have no close letter on the record, seven of them the `lemmaB-s41` units awaiting reconciliation (ev. C Table 2, NL). The one result of the period that left the program as a paper — the counterexample to Haglund's conjecture, certified by two independent producers, read by the program's blind referee agent and deposited by the sponsor on Zenodo and x67.ai (no human referee; not on arXiv; ev. D Tables 1, 3) — has exactly the post's shape: a published statement, a technique brought to it (interval certificates), and an answer anyone can check by running the deposited archive. A kill or a gap is a legitimate close under standing orders 10 and 12, and most new mechanisms die; the tally does not say the program's own objects were the wrong work. It says where, on this record, the checked and finished results have come from.
*Transfer to the RH program:* nothing that changes the standing orders: every session still runs at least one new-mechanism unit (12(a)). One addition to what a digest's ranking must show, so that the mix is chosen on the page and not by momentum: for each candidate unit, (a) whether its object is published (with the citation) or the program's own, and (b) what a second party could run to check its deliverable — a certificate, a Lean statement, an exact recomputation, or "nothing: prose". And the funding recommendation says in one line how many of the funded units are follow-ups of the program's own last result; a recommendation made only of those names at least one unit on a published object within reach of the program's instruments, or says why none is in reach. Cost: two cells and one line per digest.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the post's author was free to choose his problems and chose them for fit; this program's target is fixed by its sponsor, and a wave of units that fit the worker perfectly could leave the target untouched. The tally also has a selection effect inside it: published objects come with the definitions, the controls and the neighboring theorems already in print, so a unit on one starts further along. That is a reason the shape pays, not a reason to distrust the count.

### P2. One framework, and a toolkit that grows: reuse old tools, build new ones, keep the tools of failed projects.
*The post says:* the first assignment was to port a field's scattered methods "to a common framework, and to write the code the papers never provided" [W]; and as the work spread: "I insisted that Claude both use old tools and build new ones, so that the harness would grow. Each tool, even from a failed project, opened up new doors" [K].
*What it is, in one sentence:* code written for one problem is kept where the next problem finds it, checked once and then used, so that each project starts higher than the last.
*Already adopted here?* For results, yes: the zoo, the Instruments tables (10(k)) and the theorem register (10(q)) carry statements and quantities forward. For code, no. The inventory (ev. B1; 1,081 code files under `results/` and `scripts/`: 612 written by units, 371 by their readers, 82 infrastructure) found no index, manual or register of tools anywhere in the program — `STATUS.md` "Key artifacts" lists documents only, and the Instruments tables are defined as "quantity | current best value | result file | dated" (`directions/README.md` l. 34), so code appears there only as the file a number came from — and no rule about reusing code in `KICKSTART.md` or `BRIEF-WARNINGS.md`. What the record shows instead is the same object written again by each unit that needs it: eleven writer programs generate the system S8 in the two streams that worked on it — in `free-greedy-s40` one tool's deliberate line (the prototype, its "line-by-line C port" as a 10(l) rehearsal, the production generator and its "WINDOWED version", `compute/verify/s8_port.c` l. 1, `s8win.c` l. 1; the theory unit's `s8_check.py` carries over the prototype's core, `theory/verify/s8_check.py` l. 2) and the theory unit's own drift-free variants; in `lemmaB-s41` five units (U1, U4, U5, U6, U7) each wrote its own while validated generators existed, no two units sharing more than a quarter of their lines — beside ten more written by readers; the zero finder for a truncation F_X exists in at least four units, each its own code; arXiv query helpers in at least eleven folders; eighteen zoo-insertion scripts, one per session, though each carries its own inserted text, which B1 says "overstates rewriting" (ev. B1, Counts; Table 1, REC row). The one written rule on code is a prohibition, and it is addressed to writers: the `lemmaB-s41` charter names two existing generators "to cross-check against (never to import)" (`results/lemmaB-s41/CHARTER.md` l. 28). That is the readers' rule — a reader must not share code with the unit it checks, and 34 percent of all code files (371 of 1,081) are readers' own, by design — carried over to units that are not checking anything. The reuse that does exist is early and narrow: 21 files in five units import four modules from two units of August and September (`ccm-dh-test/dh.py` in 15 of them), and the Lean runner with its two check tools was copied byte for byte through seven units (ev. B1, Counts). The cost is on the record too. Fifteen tool defects are recorded, fourteen bugs and one stated limit (ev. B1 Table 3); one of them, the block-edge bug of a Session-40 generator, was found by a later unit's reader and changed numbers already in the record ("sup E 58.18 → 49.67 and 171.18 → 336.18", `LOG.md` l. 2286); another put the word "certified" on an ordering whose error "the code never bounds" (wave-3 digest l. 512). And the best-checked generator the program owns is known — one that "agrees cell by cell with a 60-digit mpmath brute force at 2·10⁵ and count for count with two other generators" (`results/lemmaB-s41/U6-certificate/read-O.md` l. 301, as cited in ev. B1) — with nothing that sends the next unit to it.
*Transfer to the RH program:* a tools register, on the model of the theorem register. `rh-program/TOOLS.md`: one row per reusable program — what it computes, the file, what it was validated against and by whom (a brute force, a second producer, a reader's own generator), its speed, its known limits, the units that used it. A unit's NOTE §0 ends with its TOOL ROWS as it ends with its LEDGER ROWS; a tool from a unit that closed as a kill or a gap gets its row all the same. A charter's "Read first" names the rows a writer unit should start from; a writer that writes its own version of a registered tool says in one line why. Readers are untouched: a reader still shares no code with the unit it reads. No backfill: the first rows are the validated generators and certificate producers that the Session 42 queue will use. Cost: no agent; a few rows per unit.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the post's toolkit serves many problems in many fields, so every tool has many future users; here a generator serves one constructed system and may be dead when that system is. And independence has value beyond reading: two writer units that share a generator share its bugs, and the record's agreement "count for count" between separately written generators is itself evidence. So the register does not forbid a second implementation; it ends the default of not knowing a first one exists.

### P3. Build the tool instead of grinding.
*The post says:* "Claude's default approach seemed to be to try to grind through a long, multiday calculation rather than build a new tool that would make that same calculation take mere minutes. Time and again, I had to tell it to think smarter, not harder" [T]; and in the list of tips: "The model will grind forever if you let it" [T].
*What it is, in one sentence:* before a long computation is run, somebody asks whether a better method would make it short.
*Already adopted here?* For computation, yes — and the record shows the opposite of the post's failure. Of the eight long compute legs on the record (ev. B2 Table 1), a cheaper method was found before or during the leg in three: the Lane A producers, projected by the orchestrator at "≈ 18.6 h single-process, ≈ 5 h on 4 jobs" (`LOG.md` l. 1451), ran in "Arb 14 s, mp 7.4 min" (l. 1459) once the planner saw that the row cost did not depend on the window count; the C2 campaign's contract priced 8·10⁴ zeros and 6.5 hours at the top height, and the builder's choice of radius brought it to a few hundred zeros and minutes — "overstated the campaign by ×20–50; found and fixed by the builder at zero cost" (l. 1591); the S8 generator went from a Python prototype to C and then to a windowed generator "3× faster" (ev. B2 Table 1 row 7). A smaller dress rehearsal ran first in five of the seven legs where one applies (10(l) in practice). One leg was ground through with a faster tool priced and not built: the D4 sweep, about 7.5 hours of local compute (l. 1696), with a GPU port priced for the next tier and then "made CONDITIONAL" (l. 1693) and, by the reader's search of the later log, never run. That was a reasoned decision — the port was to be funded "only when a later unit needs the instrument" at the higher bandwidth (`STATUS.md` l. 262, as cited in ev. B2) — and the sweep's own close calls it well spent. The waste lines agree: of 23 session-close waste lines, two name an agent run spent for nothing, both killed by the output ceiling, none by a computation that should have been a tool (ev. B2 Table 3).
*Transfer to the RH program:* none for computation; 10(l) and the builders' practice already do what the author had to ask for "time and again". The post's second sense — a line of ATTACK ground at session after session — has one stream on the record that could be asked about directly (`lemmaB-s41`: seven units on one lemma, proved partial results, the lemma open), and one family behind it: 16 of the 18 units of Sessions 38–41 worked on constructed systems of the program's own (Q_cond, Conjectures U and O, S5, S7, S8, Lemma B_ρ; ev. C Table 1). That is not a recorded failure — each unit closed or awaits its reads — but the instrument named below cannot yet show it: 10(q)'s register has no rows and no backfill, so the family's history enters a target table only when a charter cites it. No budget rule is proposed. The instrument that will show a grind if one develops already exists: the target table of 10(q) (unit, route, "broke at") opens when three units share a target, and rule (s) sends the stuck step to the corpus when two units stop at the same place.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the author's calculations were in fields where a known better algorithm usually existed and he could tell; the program's legs were priced and rehearsed first because its rules, bought earlier, demand it.

### P4. The model has no sense of time.
*The post says:* "Claude has no sense of time, and loves to be dramatic." After three days of work it reported "Two years of campaign". "When I ask for ETAs, the estimates are always either way too long or way too short. I tried telling Claude not to commit to an estimate until it ran a test to confirm, but that didn't work well either" [T]. In the end the author stopped asking: "I developed a sense of how long something interesting should take" [T].
*What it is, in one sentence:* elapsed time and remaining time as the model states them are not measurements, and telling it to do better does not make them so.
*Already adopted here?* For the cost of computations, yes, and it works: where an estimate was made from a measured rung it was right (the planner's Lane A projection within about ten percent; the D4 cost model "4 % low"; ev. B2 Table 2 rows 4, 8), and where a compute cost was priced in advance from a formula it was wrong by one to two orders of magnitude, too high: "×280", "×20–50", "×30" and about ×150 (rows 2, 5, 6, 3). Other advance prices were close — a zero's cost ×1.2 low, a height ceiling 10²⁰ against 6.63·10¹⁹, two slot prices on or under target, a stream's tokens 373k against 400–560k (rows 7, 9, 10, 11, 12); of the twelve pairs, seven are overstatements, three of them by ×1.5 or less or without a ratio (rows 1, 9, 12). So this program's experience differs from the author's: testing before estimating did work here, as 10(l) requires. For the clock itself, no — and the record says so again and again. The orchestrator writes time stamps from feel. Session 24's waste line: "timestamps estimated instead of read (corrected in place at 17:53 from the commit times — stamp with `date`, in the same call as the write, every time)" (`LOG.md` l. 1665). The same remedy had been written down as an intention eight sessions earlier, at Session 16's close ("(3) stamp entries with the machine clock", `LOG.md` l. 1392), and the slip is recorded in at least fourteen sessions — 16, 20, 21, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 36, 38, 39, 40, 41 (ev. B2, note to Table 2, lists eleven; Sessions 16, 20, 36 at `LOG.md` l. 1348, 1494, 2067): "seven brief headers stamped by estimate instead of from the clock (the third session running …)" (l. 2217); "four read-F headers and two briefs stamped by estimate" (l. 2277). It happened twice more in this side-session, the second time five minutes after the correction of the first had been logged (`ORCH-NOTES.md` N4). The same blind spot is written into a brief: the `lemmaB-s41` stop line tells an agent that has a proof to "try to break it for an hour" (`results/lemmaB-s41/CHARTER.md` l. 34) — a duration no agent can measure from the inside. Of the post's other half, drama, the record shows little: none of the words searched for ("breakthrough", "landmark", "remarkable") occurs in `STATUS.md` or `LOG.md`, and "campaign" there is the name of a numerical run.
*Transfer to the RH program:* (i) a stamp is produced by the command that writes the line, never typed: one helper in `scripts/` appends a stamped line to a file, and a brief's header carries a placeholder that the helper fills from the clock; the close-out check compares every stamp added in the session with the commit that introduced it and fails on a stamp later than its commit. Fourteen sessions show that the instruction alone does not hold; a mechanism does. (ii) No brief gives an agent a duration of effort. Effort is stated in things that can be counted on disk — attacks named and written to the file, attempts numbered, minutes of a process by the clock. (iii) A sharpening of 10(l): a decision NOT to run a compute leg never rests on a cost formula priced in advance; the smallest rung is run and measured first — the record's formula-priced compute estimates overstate by ×20 to ×280 (rows 2, 3, 5, 6), while its slot and token prices were close (rows 10–12).
*Why it may NOT transfer:* no disanalogy for (i) and (ii). For (iii): measuring the smallest rung costs something, and for a leg that is plainly out of reach it is waste; the rule is for decisions that an estimate within a factor of a few hundred would change.

### P5. Compaction loses context: consolidate the files so that the latest plan is always where a fresh context finds it.
*The post says:* "Over the course of these long projects, compaction would often kick in, causing Claude to lose important context. To guard against this, I had Claude periodically organize its files and consolidate them, so it always had access to the latest version of the plan" [T].
*What it is, in one sentence:* the plan is a short current document that is rewritten, and it is kept apart from the history that produced it.
*Already adopted here?* The principle, in the file's own words — and not in its practice. `STATUS.md` l. 10 defines itself: "always-current dashboard: phase state, live tasks, constraints, next actions. Overwrite freely; keep lean"; l. 52: "A fresh session should read this file top to bottom, then follow 'How to resume' at the end"; `KICKSTART.md` Part 2 item 2: "read `rh-program/STATUS.md` top to bottom". Measured by the orchestrator on 2026-10-03 from the git history (`git cat-file` at sampled commits): the file was 85 kB on 2 Sept, 150 kB on 9 Sept, 424 kB on 29 Sept and is 578 kB now — at about four bytes per token, on the order of 145k tokens to read "top to bottom" before any work. It is not a dashboard that is overwritten; it is appended to. (i) The header line (l. 26) is a chain of "Previous:" states: Session 33 trimmed it and moved 31 older entries to `LOG.md` ("the STATUS header trimmed 31.6 kB → 3.0 kB", l. 26; sampled commits show 32.0 kB at 11:09 and 6.5 kB at 14:03 IST on 29 Sept); eight sessions later it is 27 kB again. (ii) The current plan, "SESSION 42 QUEUE", starts at l. 124 under the heading "## SESSION 8 CLOSED 2026-08-26" (l. 122) and is followed by the queues of Sessions 41, 40, 39, 38, 37, 36 and earlier, each marked superseded — "stands as history"; that section is 237 kB. (iii) "Live/completed background tasks" (from l. 401) is 258 kB, almost all of it completed. (iv) The section "How to resume (fresh session checklist)" that l. 52 sends a fresh session to still describes the program's first weeks: its steps are the phase-3 designer results, the phase-4 critics and a prospectus retired on 2026-09-09; the real resume point is reached only through the header line. The same growth holds for the other files a session leans on: `LOG.md` 223 → 811 kB, `BARRIER-ZOO.md` 158 → 493 kB, `KICKSTART.md` 15 → 36 kB since 9 Sept (the log and the zoo are append-only by design and are read in windows; STATUS and KICKSTART are read whole). The trim was done once, as a housekeeping item of one queue (SESSION 33 QUEUE item 4(c)), and the current queue lists it again by hand as small bookkeeping ("STATUS housekeeping (move the older 'Previous:' header entries and …", SESSION 42 QUEUE item 4, l. 129); no rule repeats it. By the orchestrator's partition of the file (`ORCH-NOTES.md` N3) the text a fresh session needs is of the order of 45–50 kB of the 578 kB.
*Transfer to the RH program:* a bounded plan file and a rule that keeps it bounded. `STATUS.md` keeps what a fresh session must have — the protocol, the standing orders, ONE current-state paragraph, ONE queue, the entries of runs actually in flight, a resume checklist that is true today — under a size cap; everything superseded moves, verbatim and in the same commit, to an archive file that is read in windows like the log. The move is mechanical and checkable (every line of the old file is in exactly one of the two new files). Cost: no agent; one script run per session close.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* no disanalogy — the post's reason (a fresh or compacted context must find the plan) is this program's standing order 0 ("A fresh session must be able to continue from disk alone"). Two cautions. Other files cite `STATUS.md` by line number (the Cogentic study does: "l. 24", "l. 41", "l. 124"), and those citations already drift with every insertion; after the split they should cite the standing order or queue item by its number, not by line. And the split must not become a rewrite: the live text is moved, never restated (the lesson of 10(q) rule 2 and 10(t)).

### P6. The model declares victory: fix what "done" means before the work starts.
*The post says:* "Claude loves to declare victory. 'Done, with one asterisk' is often 'not done at all.' 'Exactly that, with one refinement' usually means 'no.' Giving Claude clear and rigid standards for what success looks like can help with this. On one project, it was proud of its proof, up to 'one unproven lemma.' That lemma was the whole proof! I said no unproven lemmas. Then 'done' again, but now with a new axiom" [T].
*What it is, in one sentence:* a result announced with a qualifier is to be read by its qualifier, and the standard of success is written before the work, not after.
*Already adopted here?* The standard of success, yes: 28 of the 29 briefs of Sessions 35–41 state in advance what a close must be (the T / K / G definitions, a "Lands:" line or a target theorem; ev. C Table 2, 2e), every statement carries a label, and since standing order 12(d) "a claimed proof is a GAP until read at the line". The net behind it works, and its size is now counted (ev. A): in Sessions 35–41, 43 announced statements were later corrected — 19 narrowed, 7 relabeled as resting on a printed result, 2 withdrawn, 2 with a hypothesis found false, 13 repairs of the record — against 28 announcements that held (12 of them untouched). Thirty-two of the 43 were first caught by the second model's read, 5 by the orchestrator (2 by its read-F, 3 by its own re-derivation or self-check), 6 by later units, digests or a referee agent, and the median delay was one session (ev. A, Counts; the 28 that held are those of Sessions 36–41). What is not adopted is the post's point about the qualifier, and the record has its two cases, word for word. In Session 38 a unit closed with "the general case reduced to one named lemma" (`LOG.md` l. 2158); one session later the read found that under RH the lemma "is EQUIVALENT, set by set, to Conjecture O in mean square … a reformulation, not a weaker missing input" (l. 2176), and the header records it as "Lemma G is Conjecture O restated" (`STATUS.md` l. 26). In Session 40 the header announced "a conditional theorem whose single missing lemma is the next session's target" (l. 26; in the log, "now rests on ONE qualitative integer bound, Lemma B_ρ. NOT PROVED", `LOG.md` l. 2209); Session 41 put seven units and the orchestrator's notes on that lemma and closed with "NO upper bound on E proved" (l. 26) — a first bound of another kind was proved, and the lemma is open. Of the ten conditional results on the record, one had its hypothesis refuted within a session, one was the target restated, one was a printed open conjecture, six are open, and the fate of one was not traced (ev. A Table 2, c9). And once the header went beyond the log: the unit's line read "A CANDIDATE COUNTEREXAMPLE TO CONJECTURE U, numerical" (`LOG.md` l. 2178) and the header, the text the sponsor's summary is drawn from, read "A NUMERICAL COUNTEREXAMPLE TO CONJECTURE U" (`STATUS.md` l. 26); it was withdrawn the next session, every number having reproduced (l. 2208) — the calculation was right and the conclusion was not, which is the post's sixth item to the letter. The placing of the qualifier is counted as well: of 41 announcements that were later corrected, 13 named the open part in the sentence that carried the claim, 16 named one only elsewhere in the paragraph — in 10 of those a general one ("report level", "single-check") that pointed at a different gap from the one found — and 12 named none (ev. A, "Wording at announcement").
*Transfer to the RH program:* two lines, both about wording at the moment of announcement. (i) A conditional result leads with what is open. Its row in the register and its sentence in the header begin with the open hypothesis, and say in one clause what is known of that hypothesis against the target — equivalent to it, stronger, weaker (with the reason), or not known; until a read has checked that clause, the words "one", "single" and "only" are not used of a missing piece. (ii) The header never says more than the log. A result that has not been read is "claimed" or "candidate" in every place it appears, and the words "counterexample", "refuted", "proved" and "certified" stand in the header only next to the checks that earned them; this goes into `BRIEF-WARNINGS.md` W3 as a line for the orchestrator, with the Session-39 header as its evidence. Cost: none.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* no disanalogy. One caution from the count itself: the record corrects more statements than it leaves untouched, almost always within a session, so a qualifier-free header would be the wrong lesson — the qualifiers were mostly there ("single-check", "report level", "pending the reads"); what failed in the cases above was their place in the sentence and the judgment of how much the open part weighed.

### P7. Look at the data yourself: plots, and no qualitative claims of agreement.
*The post says:* "Look at everything yourself. I always ask to see plots. Even with all the monitors I set up, I've found the automated checks still can't be trusted. Beware of qualitative claims like 'good agreement.'" And: "Question the conclusions. Claude is good at performing calculations, but the conclusions it draws can be wrong. Have it explain what it found until you believe it" [T].
*What it is, in one sentence:* the person responsible looks at the raw result in a form the eye can judge, and treats the sentence drawn from a computation as a claim separate from the computation.
*Already adopted here?* The second half, thoroughly. A reader re-runs every decisive computation with its own code and tests every label (`results/novel-wave-s41/READ-BRIEF-O.md` steps 2–3, as cited in the Cogentic study §B); every statement carries one of four labels, with "[computed]" tied to a script and log on disk (`results/lemmaB-s41/CHARTER.md` §4); `BRIEF-WARNINGS.md` W2 and W3 name the two failures of conclusion (a fit stated as an exponent; a label stronger than its check); 10(r) forbids a stop on a fit. The first half — looking — is absent in one exact sense: the program has never drawn its own data. Checked by the orchestrator on 2026-10-03: no file under `results/`, `scripts/` or `directions/` (code, TeX or notes; literature folders excluded) contains a call to any plotting tool (`matplotlib|pyplot|savefig|plt.`, `gnuplot`, terminal plotters, `pgfplots`/`tikzpicture`, Wolfram `ListPlot`/`Plot[`, `seaborn|plotly|bokeh`: 0 files each), and all 76 image files under `results/` are page scans of printed sources (`…/lit/img/haglund-p-08.png`, `…/verify-O/bombhi-7b.png`, `…/pa/…`, `…/pages/…`) or screenshots of the landing page (`results/x67-landing-s41/`). `matplotlib` 3.9.4 is installed on the machine. Meanwhile the numerical error that repeats most on the record is the one a picture shows at a glance. In the wave-3 digest's errata (`results/novel-wave-s39/insights-digest.md` §E, l. 465–513): "'β ≈ 0.30' is the slope of the running sup on [10³, 10⁹]" (E.3, l. 472); the unit had written "clean power laws, not transients" and "the brief's stop condition … is met" (E.3, l. 475); "'β = 0 numerically; no power law fits' overstated nine running-max points" (E.9 F2, l. 513); "'provably log-powers' is a fit (κ ≈ 2.3–3)" (E.2 F4, l. 470); a constant's range misstated by a factor, "(0.37–0.53)·ρ·log²x" for (0.20–0.37) (E.8 F3, l. 508); a quoted gap that "do[es] not reproduce — a quadrature artifact" (E.5 F1, l. 490). Each was caught — by a reader, after the sentence was in a NOTE; and one of them after it had reached the sponsor: Session 39's header announced "A NUMERICAL COUNTEREXAMPLE TO CONJECTURE U (… β ≈ 0.30, α ≈ 0.75 …)" and Session 40's records it "WITHDRAWN" (`STATUS.md` l. 26). The post's own example phrase is not the program's: "good agreement" and "excellent agreement" occur nowhere in `STATUS.md`, `LOG.md` or any `NOTE*.md`; the program's cousin of it is "consistent with" (31 times in NOTE files, 10 in `LOG.md`, 5 in `STATUS.md`, by case-insensitive grep), and 10(g)'s lint list ("clearly / obviously / easy to see / well known") has words about proofs and none about data.
*Transfer to the RH program:* (i) a NUMERICAL claim over a range ships its picture — the raw points, the claimed law drawn through them, and a second panel with the residuals or the local slope per decade — made by the unit's script and saved beside the NOTE; the reader's re-run draws its own; (ii) the orchestrator's read at the line LOOKS at both pictures (the session's model reads images) and writes one line on what it sees, before any sentence about the claim goes into STATUS or to the sponsor; (iii) a numerical headline reported to the sponsor carries the picture's path — he has said he will not referee mathematics, but nine points with a line through them look like nine points to anyone; (iv) the lint list of 10(g) gains the data words — "consistent with", "agrees with", "matches", "as expected", "confirms", "stable" — each allowed only with the number, the tolerance and the range in the same sentence. Cost: a few lines of plotting code per numerical unit; no agent. One mechanical point: `.gitignore` drops every `results/**/*.png` ("A figure the program makes itself needs its own '!' line"), so the rule names a folder for the program's own figures and adds its negation line.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the post's plots set data against models in empirical fields; the program's numerical objects (integer errors and running sups of constructed systems to 10¹¹, zero locations, certificate margins) are also data against a claimed law, so the analogy holds for statements of kind NUMERICAL and for nothing else — a picture proves nothing, and W2 extends to it: no close and no stop rests on a picture. A log–log plot flatters every power law; that is why the second panel (residuals or local slope) is part of the rule and not an option.

### P8. Taste: the model's judgment of what is interesting cannot be trusted.
*The post says:* "Supply the taste. Claude can find Claude-shaped problems, but there are thousands, perhaps millions, of them. Claude seems to favor old debates, highly cited but long forgotten. Asking it to focus on what is newly possible, not what is merely faster or involves more digits, helps, but you still can't trust its judgment of whether something is interesting" [T]. Of his earlier experiment (last December, before he changed method): "I had to … steer it away from irrelevant threads, and pull it back from dead ends" [W].
*What it is, in one sentence:* the model will always have a next thing to work on, and its sense of which next thing matters is the faculty the author found least reliable.
*Already adopted here?* The program judges three things about a candidate unit and never this one as it bears on anyone outside the program (inside, 10(a) ranks "the three most useful findings" and routes are chosen "on merit", `STATUS.md` l. 35). Every funding rule on the record is a test of correctness, of form, or of newness of route: a theorem surviving two reads, a new control, a Lean-checked statement, a route that "starts beyond the ground the zoo already marks as covered", a "NEW mechanism" (ev. D Table 4, seven rows; `KICKSTART.md` 10(d); `STATUS.md` l. 35, l. 44). The one written test of whether a result is worth something to anyone outside was made in August, for the papers, in answer to the sponsor's own question — "it's pointless if the paper carries nothing novel and doesn't contribute to the field, right?" — and the program's answer was a good one: a negative result earns its place "when it stops someone else wasting time", sorted by the question "Would anyone otherwise have tried this?", with the audience named (`CIRCULATION-PREP.md` l. 249–258). It was applied once, to those four papers; ev. D found it applied to no unit, digest or queue since, and found the question "what would a specialist ask instead" nowhere in 814 files. What chooses the work in its place is the reallocation rule: 18 of the last 29 units are follow-ups of the program's own previous result (P1), as 10(d) requires of a graded result ("the budget belongs to the follow-ups of (a)", wave-3 digest l. 553), and the rule that would tie a unit back to the program's target is observed in form only — 10(g) says "every brief names the clause it discharges"; no brief of Sessions 35–41 names a numbered clause of a direction's contract theorem (0 of 29), while nine of them carry a heading "Contract clause (what this unit discharges)" under which the text is the unit's own target (ev. C Table 2, 2d; for example `results/free-greedy-s40/theory/BRIEF.md` l. 5–6). The post's particular complaint — old, much-cited debates; faster and more digits — is on this record up to Session 35: it is the sponsor's stated reason for standing order 12 ("the earlier sessions focused too much on existing human mathematicians' research and how they do things", `STATUS.md` l. 44). Since Session 36 the drift runs the other way, toward objects the program made itself the week before — in part the intended effect of 12(a); a rule that pushes the mix back toward published objects must not reopen the bias 12(a) closed.
*Transfer to the RH program:* no agent can supply taste, and the note does not pretend one can; two lines make the choice visible to whoever does. (i) The bearing line. Every charter and brief states, where 10(g) wants its clause, either the numbered clause of a direction's contract that the unit discharges, or — for a unit on an object of the program's own — the chain from that object back to the program's target, in numbered steps, each marked proved, conjectured or heuristic, and what each possible close would change in the next queue. A unit whose every close changes nothing is not launched. (ii) The August question, in the only form a model can answer: each candidate in a digest's ranking has one more cell, "who outside the program has worked on this object or asked this question — the citation — or 'no one: the program's own object'". That is a fact a reader can check; whether anyone would care is not, and §C.4 keeps that judgment out of agents. Cost: one line per brief, one cell per candidate.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the author's remedy was himself, and then experts; the program has neither kind of judge in its loop (P9), so these lines inform a choice that is still made by the model the post says not to trust. They do not fix that. They make the chain and the audience of each unit something the sponsor can read in plain words, and something a later reader can hold the unit to.

### P9. The expert who expects "a shrug" from the field — and then reframes the question.
*The post says:* outside his own field the author could not tell a good result from a dull one — "I find myself agreeing" — and what settled it, "in almost all cases" [K], was a person who works in the field. Of the ecology result, the expert said it would "be met with a shrug by many ecologists", and then "had a better idea: subtract the neutral prediction and study the remainder" [K]. The pattern, in the author's words: "Claude comes up with an initial finding I find compelling. I bring it to an expert, who is unmoved but sees the potential, and together we sculpt it into meaningful science" [K]. Experts were not easy to get: "I had to write to three different biologists for validation before one responded" [K].
*What it is, in one sentence:* correctness can be checked from the inside; whether a correct result matters, and what the better question is, came, in the post's cases, from someone outside who works in the subject.
*Already adopted here?* The inside half, completely; the outside half once. Inside: dual reads, two producers, Lean, and for every outgoing text a referee — each of them an agent of the program ("No human referee of any outgoing text was found", ev. D Table 3, nine rows). Outside: one letter. The courtesy note on [ÁLKL23] was sent by the sponsor on 2026-09-07 to that paper's three authors, and its first author answered on 2026-09-18; the program's own summary of the answer is "about half the arguments read, 'seem to be OK', full reading expected next week; two questions" (`LOG.md` l. 1634). That is the only human reader other than the sponsor on the whole record (ev. D Table 2, with the scope and patterns it searched), and it came eleven days after the one time the program wrote to experts. What happened to it afterwards is also on the record: an answer was drafted the same day and headed "as sent or to be sent by the sponsor", with no line saying that it went (ev. D Table 2 row 3); the item "the Álvarez López reply watch stays OPEN" stands in the SESSION 39 QUEUE (`STATUS.md` l. 150) and in no later one — by the orchestrator's count of 2026-10-03 the queues of Sessions 38 and 39 each name the reply watch and the arXiv endorsement once, and the queues of Sessions 40, 41 and 42 name neither; no line closes either item, and the current queue's sponsor item opens "nothing is required" (l. 128). For the rest: three papers are public, each by the sponsor's act, on Zenodo and x67.ai (ev. D Table 1 rows 1–4); the record shows no reader, reply, citation or download count for any of them (Table 2 row 5); none is on arXiv — "Still outstanding, and only the sponsor can do it: arXiv endorsement" (`results/arxiv/README.md` l. 159–160, as cited in ev. D), with no line recording that an endorser was asked (row 6); and no contact is recorded with the authors whose conjectures or theorems the papers treat, the author of the conjecture that the third paper refutes among them (row 7).
*Transfer to the RH program:* one rule, and one thing that is not a rule. (i) The rule: what waits on the sponsor stays on the page. `STATUS.md` carries one short list, "With the sponsor", of every item only he can move — a letter owed or awaited, the endorsement, a decision asked of him — and each item is carried forward word for word until a dated line closes it with its reason. A reply is an input and never a gate (standing order 10(c)); an input that drops out of the queue without a closing line is an input lost, and that is what the record shows happened here. (ii) Not a rule, because it is the sponsor's ground: the post's author got the judgment that turned correct results into ones that mattered from experts he wrote to, and this program's one letter was answered. Whether to write again — the answer drafted on 2026-09-18, a courtesy note to the author of the conjecture the third paper refutes, a request for an arXiv endorsement — goes out under his name and is his to decide; the program's part is to keep each draft ready and to say so to him in plain words, once.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the post's experts were colleagues within reach of a professor at their own university; the sponsor has no such standing and has said that the technical side is not his. A cold letter may get no answer — the post's own count is three written to for one reply — and an answer may be "correct, and of no interest", which is exactly the information the program cannot produce for itself. Nothing may wait for a reply (standing order 10(c)).

### P10. Follow up; and lift the limits the model sets itself.
*The post says:* "Follow up. Once Claude has a great result, ask for an even greater one. It will always come up with something, and occasionally it's brilliant" [T]. And from the first project: asked for unsolved cases, the model found few, and "it became clear that Claude was limiting itself" to the simplest family of functions; the author asked "could it do the same thing for the next simplest family", and it could [W].
*What it is, in one sentence:* after a success, ask for the stronger statement; and ask what restriction the worker put on the problem without being told to.
*Already adopted here?* The first half is the program's default. 10(d) pulls the next session's budget into the follow-ups of a graded result, and it is used: of fourteen positive closes in Sessions 35–41, nine were followed by a funded unit — the same result strengthened (the Haglund counterexample certified and written up; Theorem R formalized in Lean), the next class, or the result's own missing lemma (ev. C Table 3). The follow-ups that slide are of one kind: the Lean statements queued for Theorem T and for U_q, L′ and D were named in three successive queues and not run (the last Lean folder is `theoremR-lean-s36`; ev. C Table 3 rows 3, 6, 9). The second half is on the record as a reader's finding, not as a question anyone asks: in fifteen cases a read or a digest found that a unit had delivered less than its brief asked, a special case of it, or a claim that had to be cut back — a partition "by inequality, not by input" where the charter asked for one by input; "E = o(x) NOT obtained" where the charter said "first E = o(x)"; an exclusion "narrowed to the §7.1 families" (ev. C Table 4). The reads catch it. Nothing asks the unit to say it.
*Transfer to the RH program:* one line in the close of every NOTE, checked by the reads with the rest: "Asked / delivered" — what the brief asked, what was delivered, and every restriction the unit placed on the problem that the brief did not (a smaller class, a range, an added hypothesis), each with its reason. The next brief on the same object starts from that line. Cost: one line per unit. Nothing else: the follow-up rule itself is already ours (§B).
*Why it may NOT transfer:* in the post the limit was a matter of scope — the next family of functions was within reach of the same machinery. Here a restriction is often forced by the mathematics, and "the next class" may be the open problem. The line does not ask for the wider statement; it asks that the narrowing be said by the one who made it.

### P11. The setup: a master session, one session per project, a separate adversarial referee, subagents as containment.
*The post says:* "I have separate sessions for each project, plus a master session that coordinates the others, allocates compute, and validates results. Each session involves agents that run the computations in the background, with intermediate results stored in markdown files in their respective folders." Subagents also limit damage: when a safety classifier fires, "instead of these blocks corrupting my whole session, they just shut down a single agent." And there are separate sessions for writing, for tools and manuals, and for "checking and rechecking results as an adversarial referee" [T].
*What it is, in one sentence:* coordination, production and refereeing are kept in separate contexts, state lives in files, and a failure is confined to the agent it happens in.
*Already adopted here?* Yes, in every part. One orchestrating session coordinates and reads; units run as background agents that write their NOTE, their scripts and `SHARED.md` as they go (standing order 0; 10(e); item 16's write-first lines); the referee is a separate agent that may not import the unit's code (`READ-BRIEF-O.md` step 3), and outgoing papers get a blind referee agent (the Haglund manuscript: "BLIND-REFEREED (MINOR REVISION; the mathematics holds …)", `STATUS.md` l. 26). Containment is the reason behind two standing rules: standing order 3 as amended ("Three usage-limit deaths in one day each killed ten or more agents in flight", `STATUS.md` l. 33) and item 16 (an agent that died at the output ceiling "with nothing on disk", then the write-first clause). The one classifier event on the record is of another kind — the harness's permission classifier, not a model safeguard — and was handled as a denial of the outcome, not routed around: "the auto-mode classifier denied the program's push (twice; the denial covers the outcome, so no other route was taken)" (`LOG.md`, Session 39 entry). One difference of regime: this program's orchestrator is rebuilt from `STATUS.md` at every session, which is why P5 weighs heavily here.
*Transfer to the RH program:* none; corroboration, recorded in §B.

### P12. The outlook: increments, the sentence on Millennium problems, the convex hull.
*The post says:* progress is built "in increments, each one resting on the last" [O]. Of problems of this program's kind it has two passages. The opening: the models' successes "so far these have mostly been well-scoped applications of existing techniques", and "Many of the headlines seem to be in mathematics, the one part of science where a problem can be stated completely and an answer checked absolutely" [I] — the shape of the program's own finished results (P1), and a caution for the new-mechanism units of standing order 12(a) that this note records and does not act on. The outlook: "The focus on Millennium Prize Problems and Big Science may be, as Claude likes to say, a 'footgun'", the risk named being that "unrealistic expectations may discourage productive uses that are already possible" [O]. Its picture of where the model is strongest is the convex hull of what is known: "The middle regions, where humans could reach but no particular human has, are ideal for AI" [O]. And: "humans are still needed for the conceptual part" [O].
*What it is, in one sentence:* the author's advice on where to aim — at the reachable middle, by accumulation — offered as his judgment after three months, with no experiment behind the sentence on large targets.
*Already adopted here?* The target is not this note's to weigh: it is fixed by the sponsor (standing orders 10 and 12), and standing order 14 forbids sentences whose only work is to report on its status. What can be said from the record is narrower and is already in P1: the results of this program that are checked, finished and public are increments of exactly the post's kind — three papers, each on a published object, each of them something a reader can verify — and they came out of work aimed at the large target. On this record the two are not in competition; the increments are what the attack leaves behind. The "middle region" has its instance too: the Haglund certificate joined a 2009 conjecture in one corner to interval arithmetic in another.
*Transfer to the RH program:* none beyond P1's two cells. The register of 10(q) is the program's ledger of increments "each one resting on the last", and it opened with no rows at 00:29 IST the same night (commit 63c22928), between one and one and a half hours before this note was written.
*Why it may NOT transfer:* the sentence is about what expectations do to people who might otherwise use the tools; it is not a finding about what a long program aimed at one target can or cannot produce, and the post contains no such program.

## §A. The rules as proposed — KICKSTART Part 2 item 10, letters (u)–(z)

PROPOSED, not applied. Each is a file, a line or a script; none needs an agent and none assumes width. Each answers a failure on the program's own record, cited in the block named. Where a script can hold the rule, the rule is the script: ev. C shows what happens to a rule that lives only in the manual (10(g): the heading survives in nine briefs, the clause in none).

**(u) The plan file is bounded (from P5, P9).**
`STATUS.md` holds what a fresh session needs and nothing else: the protocol, the standing orders, ONE paragraph of current state, ONE queue, the task entries of the newest session, a resume checklist that is true today, and a short list "With the sponsor". At every session close `scripts/status-split.py` moves everything superseded, verbatim and in the same commit, to `STATUS-ARCHIVE.md`, and prints its check (every line of the old file is in exactly one of the two); the hashes go into the closing LOG entry. The archive is read in windows, like the log, never whole. A session that finds `STATUS.md` above 80 kB runs the split before anything else. Other files cite a standing order or a queue item by its number, never `STATUS.md` by line. "With the sponsor" lists every item only he can move — a letter owed or awaited, an endorsement, a decision asked of him; each stays word for word until a dated line closes it with its reason, and a queue that drops one is returned. (The post [T]: files consolidated so that the model "always had access to the latest version of the plan"; record: 85 kB → 578 kB in a month, the live queue under a heading of 26 August, a resume checklist that describes August, two open items with the sponsor gone from three successive queues without a closing line.)

**(v) A picture for every numerical claim; data words on the lint list (from P7).**
A statement of kind NUMERICAL over a range ships a two-panel picture made by the unit's own script — the raw points with the claimed law drawn through them, and the residuals or the local slope per decade — saved in the unit's `figures/` folder (`.gitignore` gets the negation line). The reader's re-run draws its own. The orchestrator's read at the line looks at both and writes one line on what it sees before the claim enters `STATUS.md` or a report; a numerical headline given to the sponsor names the picture's path. No close and no stop rests on a picture (W2 extends to it). The lint list of 10(g) gains "consistent with", "agrees with", "matches", "as expected", "confirms", "stable": each is allowed only with the number, the tolerance and the range in the same sentence. (The post [T]: "I always ask to see plots"; "Beware of qualitative claims"; record: no plotting call in 1,081 code files; six numerical statements of one wave corrected by readers, one of them after it had been announced as a counterexample.)

**(w) The clock is read, never recalled; effort is counted, never timed (from P4).**
A time stamp is produced by `scripts/stamp.py` — a placeholder filled in a brief or header, or a stamped line appended — and never typed. `stamp.py --check <the session's first commit>` runs at the close; its output goes into the closing LOG entry, and a stamp later than the commit that introduced it is corrected before the close. No brief gives an agent a duration of effort ("for an hour"): effort is stated in what can be counted on disk — attacks named and written to the file, attempts numbered, minutes of a process by the clock. And 10(l) gains one sentence: a decision NOT to run a compute leg never rests on a cost formula priced in advance; the smallest rung is run and measured first. (The post [T]: "Claude has no sense of time"; record: stamps written from feel in at least fourteen sessions, thirteen of them after the remedy was first written down in Session 16, and twice more in this one; four formula-priced compute estimates overstated by ×20 to ×280, while slot and token prices were close.)

**(x) An announcement says what is open first, and never more than the log (from P6, P10).**
A conditional result leads with its open hypothesis: its row in the register and its sentence in the header begin with what is not proved and say in one clause how that hypothesis stands to the target — equivalent, stronger, weaker (with the reason) or not known; until a read has checked that clause, "one", "single" and "only" are not used of a missing piece. A result that has not been read is "claimed" or "candidate" wherever it appears, and "counterexample", "refuted", "proved" and "certified" stand in the header only beside the checks that earned them; `BRIEF-WARNINGS.md` W3 gains this as its ORCHESTRATOR line. Every NOTE §0 carries one line "Asked / delivered": what the brief asked, what was delivered, and every restriction the unit put on the problem that the brief did not, with its reason. (The post [T]: "one unproven lemma … That lemma was the whole proof!"; record: "the exact missing lemma" found to be the target restated; "single missing lemma" open after seven units; a header that dropped the log's word "candidate"; fifteen narrowings found by reads and none stated by the unit.)

**(y) The tools register (from P2).**
`rh-program/TOOLS.md` is the register of programs later work may start from: one row per tool — what it computes, the file, what it was validated against and by whom, its speed, its known limits, the units that used it. Every unit's NOTE §0 ends with its TOOL ROWS as it ends with its LEDGER ROWS; a tool from a unit that closed as a kill or a gap gets its row all the same. A charter's "Read first" names the rows a writer should start from, and a writer that builds its own version of a registered tool says in one line why. A reader shares no code with the unit it reads, as before. No backfill: the first rows are entered when a charter first needs them. (The post [K]: "Each tool, even from a failed project, opened up new doors"; record: five units of one stream each writing its own S8 generator beside validated ones, no index of tools, a writers' charter that says "never to import", fourteen recorded tool bugs.)

**(z) Bearing and audience, checked before launch (from P1, P8; amends 10(g)).**
Every charter and brief carries a bearing line: the numbered clause of a direction's contract that the unit discharges, or — for a unit on an object of the program's own — the chain from that object to the program's target in numbered steps, each marked proved, conjectured or heuristic, and what each possible close would change in the next queue. A unit whose every close changes nothing is not launched. Each candidate in a digest's ranking gains three cells: its object (published, with the citation, or the program's own); what a second party could run to check its deliverable; and who outside the program has worked on its object or asked its question, with the citation — or "no one: the program's own object". The funding recommendation says how many of its units are follow-ups of the program's own last result. Standing order 12(a) is untouched. `scripts/check-brief.py` fails a charter or brief that lacks a line this item requires (the pointer of 10(p), the `SOURCES.md` of 10(s), the stop line of 10(m), the bearing line, the output clause of item 16, a filled stamp, no duration of effort); the orchestrator runs it before every launch and puts its output in the live entry. (The post [T]: "you still can't trust its judgment of whether something is interesting"; record: 0 of 29 briefs name a contract clause; 18 of 29 units follow the program's own last result; the four clean theorem closes are all on published objects; the August question "Would anyone otherwise have tried this?" asked once and not again.)

## §B. Already ours — where the post corroborates an existing rule

- **Separate contexts for coordinating, producing and refereeing; state in files** (the orchestrating session; background agents writing their NOTE and `SHARED.md`; a reader that shares no code with its unit; standing order 0, 10(e)) are the post's master session, per-project sessions, "intermediate results stored in markdown files" [T] and a separate "adversarial referee" [T].
- **The standard of success written before the work** (28 of 29 briefs; the T / K / G closes; 10(c)) is "clear and rigid standards for what success looks like" [T].
- **Measure before estimating** (10(l): a smaller rung first) is what the author tried to obtain by instruction and could not; here it is a rule with a rehearsal behind it, and both estimates made from a measured rung were right (P4; two rows of B2 Table 2).
- **The better method instead of the long run** (three of the record's long legs; P3) is "think smarter, not harder" [T], done by the builders unasked.
- **Known answers first** (10(b), the ladder; the reader's independent re-run) is the post's first result: "15 reproductions of known results by this new method and 15 that had never before been computed" [W].
- **Follow-ups funded by a graded result** (10(d); nine of fourteen positive closes followed up) is "Once Claude has a great result, ask for an even greater one" [T].
- **Conclusions questioned by someone other than the one who drew them** (the dual reads; W2, W3; 43 statements corrected against 28 that held) is "Question the conclusions" [T] — with a second model in place of the author.
- **A result a second party can check by running it** (two independent producers for every certificate; the deposited archive of the Haglund paper; Lean with the comparator pair) is the post's "checkable" [W] problem, verified "by running two scripts" [W].
- **Failures confined to one agent** (standing order 3 as amended; item 16) is the post's use of subagents so that a stopped agent does not take the session with it [T].
- **A denial respected as a denial of the outcome** (Session 39's push; this session's history rewrite) has no counterpart in the post and is recorded here because it happened twice.

## §C. Explicitly NOT to copy

1. **Width across problems.** "36 manuscripts in 18 fields with 19 coauthors over three months" [T] is a regime of many small targets. The program has one; the refusals of width in item 10 stand.
2. **Choosing the problem for its fit to the worker.** That is the post's method; for the target it is not available — the target is the sponsor's (standing orders 10, 12) — but the program "chooses its routes on merit and on its own evidence" (standing order 4 as amended, `STATUS.md` l. 35), and among routes fit to the worker is a legitimate criterion (12(b)). P1 takes the part that survives — showing the shape and the object of each candidate on the page.
3. **A person as the clock and as the taste.** "I developed a sense of how long something interesting should take" [T]; "Supply the taste" [T]. The sponsor has said in writing that technical questions are not to be put to him. Rule (w) puts the clock in a script; nothing replaces the taste (P8).
4. **An agent cast as the outside expert.** Considered for P9 — a reader briefed to say whether a specialist would care — and declined: the post's own finding is that "you still can't trust its judgment of whether something is interesting" [T], and such a reader would be that judgment under another name. The outside reader is a person or no one.
5. **A budget rule against grinding at one target.** Declined for want of a recorded failure (P3): one stream has worked on one lemma, and it produced proved partial results. The target table of 10(q) is what would show a grind; two units breaking at the same step already trigger rule (s).
6. **Asking the model how long something will take.** The author gave up on it; the record's formula-priced compute estimates were wrong by one to two orders of magnitude (its slot and token prices were close). The program measures (10(l), rule (w)) and does not ask.
7. **Reading the post's results as evidence about this program's target.** Several are, in its own words, "undergoing further exploration and verification" [K]; it gives no count of what failed beyond 400 candidates and 36 manuscripts; and none of its problems is of this kind.
8. **Reading its sentence on Millennium problems as an instruction.** It is the author's view of what expectations do; the target is fixed by the sponsor and this note leaves it there (P12).

## §D. What the post says about the program's constraint

The program's constraint is a lean budget, no expert in the loop, and a sponsor who is not a specialist and has said so. Four things in the post speak to it. (1) Cost. The author calls his own projects "compute- and token-intensive" [T]; nothing in the post argues for more agents here, and one measured saving is on the table: a session that read the 578 kB status file top to bottom, as KICKSTART item 2 says, would spend on the order of 145k tokens before it starts; what sessions actually read at boot is not measured anywhere, and the 62–70 percent at which Sessions 36–41 closed is the RULE ZERO handover threshold, not a cost of the file (ev. B2 Table 5). Rule (u) bounds the worst case. (2) Who catches the errors. In the post it is the author, looking at everything himself. Here it is the second model: of 43 corrections in Sessions 35–41 the Opus read found 32 first and the orchestrator 5 (its read-F 2, its own re-derivation or self-check 3), with errors on the record that the orchestrator's read had passed (ev. A, Counts). The Cogentic study said the same from a smaller count and left the arrangement to the sponsor, whose standing order it is; this note adds the count and changes nothing. (3) The sponsor's seat. Outside his field the author found himself agreeing with whatever the model called a fine result, and what protected him was experts. The sponsor sits in that seat for every result of this program. What the program can give him from the inside is words that do not outrun the checks (rule (x)), pictures he can look at without refereeing anything (rule (v)), and for each unit a plain statement of what it is for and who outside has worked on its object (rule (z)). (4) What it cannot give him is the expert. One letter to experts has gone out in the life of the program, and it was answered (P9). That ground is his.
